title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Attackers crossed from a wind farm into an unrelated Polish CHP plant over a private cellular APN — and stopped its steam turbine
items.content_text: CERT Polska has disclosed that attackers reached the control network of a Polish combined heat and power plant serving roughly 50,000 residents by pivoting through a private cellular APN, and stopped a steam turbine and the plant’s process-water treatment system. The intrusion started somewhere else entirely: a compromised FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, and a Teltonika cellular router on that network which reached a private APN operated by the distribution system operator. Because devices on that APN were permitted to talk to one another, the attacker crossed from one generator’s network into another operator’s controllers. CERT Polska believes this is the first observed real-world use of a private APN as a route into an industrial control network. Plant staff restored the affected systems quickly and customers saw no loss of supply.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT Polska disclosure — via Help Net Security, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incident Dec 2025; disclosed 8 Aug 2026, analysis published 11–13 Aug 2026

items.title: The Iranian-affiliated PLC campaign is an energy-sector problem too, and at one victim the actors disabled safety shutdown logic
items.content_text: Joint advisory AA26-097A — issued 7 April by the FBI, CISA, NSA, EPA, DOE, US Cyber Command’s Cyber National Mission Force and Treasury, and substantially expanded on 22 July — covers Iranian-affiliated actors reaching internet-exposed programmable logic controllers across US water, energy and government facilities. Two details matter for power operators. First, the observed manufacturer scope now runs beyond Rockwell Automation to Schneider Electric and Siemens controllers, so a utility that standardised away from MicroLogix is not automatically outside it. Second, at one confirmed US victim the actors modified ladder logic to disable safety shutdown and alarm functions, letting unsafe conditions develop without alerting operators. The agencies also documented project-file exfiltration and Dropbear SSH persistence. No CVE is involved: the entry path is exposure plus default, shared or absent credentials.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA/FBI joint advisory AA26-097A — corroborated by SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Issued 7 Apr 2026, updated 22 Jul 2026; campaign ongoing through mid-Aug 2026

items.title: Clop has named 43 PTC Windchill victims including Shell and GE, and what it took is engineering data
items.content_text: The Clop extortion group has listed 43 organisations on its leak site after a mass data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM product-lifecycle instances, exploiting CVE-2026-12569, an improper input validation flaw. Ransom-ISAC assesses with high confidence that Clop affiliates ran it as a zero-day in early June, weeks before PTC began issuing patches on 17 June. Clop claims 89 GB from Shell, including engineering drawings, facility test reports and project plans; Philips has confirmed an enterprise server breach it says was contained, and GE says it is assessing the claim. BleepingComputer reports Clop built a custom web shell for the campaign. For energy operators the exposure is not the plant floor but the design record — drawings, test reports and vendor configuration that make a later, targeted intrusion far easier.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Clop leak-site listings — reported by BleepingComputer and TechTimes
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploited from early Jun 2026; victims named 15–17 Aug 2026

items.title: CISA added the exploited vCenter flaw to KEV on 18 August — the campaign has hit 361 hosts in 47 countries
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-59310, a path-traversal flaw in VMware vCenter Server, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August. Broadcom patched it on 29 July; exploitation started roughly five days later. German incident-response firm QUIRSO assesses with moderate confidence that a Chinese-speaking actor is behind the campaign, based on Chinese-language artefacts in the attacker’s scripts and tooling, and counts about 361 affected addresses across 47 countries, with Germany, the United States, Turkey, Iran and France most represented. The actor obtains root on the vCenter appliance, installs a backdoor via cron and a reverse SSH binary, and in at least one case deployed Babuk-derived ransomware. Utilities that host EMS, historian or engineering-workstation virtual machines on vCenter should treat this as an OT-adjacent exposure, not an IT one.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalogue and QUIRSO research — via The Hacker News
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Patched 29 Jul 2026; exploitation from early Aug; added to KEV 18 Aug 2026

items.title: Roughly 6,300 ICS and building-automation devices around US data centres answer from the internet — and the newer sites are the worse offenders
items.content_text: Trend Micro’s TrendAI research, published on 18 August, identified about 6,300 internet-reachable industrial control and building-automation devices in and around data centre facilities across the United States. The counter-intuitive finding is the distribution: exposure concentrates in newer builds rather than legacy estate, which the researchers attribute to the volume of connected power, cooling and monitoring equipment commissioned at speed. The devices in scope govern power distribution and cooling. For a utility the interest is not the tenant’s risk but the load: hyperscale and colocation sites are very large, tightly clustered interconnected loads whose controllers sit outside the utility’s own visibility, so an abrupt or coordinated change in their behaviour is a grid-operations question as much as a data-centre one. This is exposure research, not evidence of compromise.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: TrendAI / Trend Micro research — reported by Industrial Cyber

items.title: CISA and the FBI put Medusa past 500 critical-infrastructure victims — and say it weaponises new flaws inside 24 hours
items.content_text: The updated #StopRansomware advisory AA25-071A, reissued on 18 August by CISA and the FBI, puts Medusa’s cumulative critical-infrastructure victim count above 500 as of April 2026, up from roughly 300 in the March 2025 version — about 200 new victims in a year. Named sectors are healthcare, critical manufacturing, the defense industrial base, government facilities, IT and financial services; impact is enterprise encryption plus data theft, and no control-system involvement is alleged. The operationally useful finding is the tempo: the agencies assess Medusa turns newly disclosed vulnerabilities into working access within about 24 hours, and has been observed using exploits up to a week before public disclosure, because it buys exploits rather than developing them. For a utility that plans patching around monthly change windows, that is the number to argue with — the exposure window on an internet-facing appliance is now shorter than most emergency-change processes.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA/FBI #StopRansomware advisory AA25-071A (updated) — corroborated by The Record and BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Update published 18 Aug 2026; victim tally current to Apr 2026

items.title: SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced ships a Node-RED interface with no authentication — unauthenticated code execution at maximum severity
items.content_text: In its August Patch Tuesday round Siemens published ten advisories, the most serious of which (SSA-834709) covers SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed. The Node-RED HTTP interface does not enforce authentication, so a remote unauthenticated attacker can reach programming nodes that execute system commands and create flows that run arbitrary code on the device with maximum privileges. Siemens rates it at the top of the scale and has released a fixed version. IoT2050 gateways are common in energy applications as edge data-collection and protocol-translation points between substation or generation equipment and a historian or cloud service, which means a device that is trusted by the control network but frequently managed outside it.

items.title: A CVSS 10.0 command injection gives unauthenticated root on Haiwell’s IoT Cloud HMI gateway
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02 covers CVE-2026-19188, an OS command injection in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway rated 10.0. The Net Check feature reached through the /setting endpoint passes user-supplied input from the cmdPing Socket.io event to the operating system without sanitisation, so an unauthenticated remote attacker can run arbitrary commands as root. Version 3.40.1.12 is affected and Haiwell has published Scada-v3.50.1.19 as the fix. Haiwell gear turns up in smaller generation sites, DER installations and balance-of-plant systems where it was chosen on cost, and it is exactly the class of device that ends up on a cellular connection for remote monitoring — the same pattern behind this month’s utility intrusions.

items.title: Two energy-sector advisories from 13 August ship without a fix: Hitachi Energy APM Edge and Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808
items.content_text: ICSA-26-225-04 covers Hitachi Energy APM Edge version 6.10 and earlier, where CVE-2026-43284 (CVSS 8.8, with a scope change) and CVE-2026-43500 (7.8) allow a local user to escalate privilege. There is no fixed version. Hitachi Energy’s guidance is mitigation only: disable the esp4, esp6 and rxrpc kernel modules. ICSA-26-225-06 covers Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 — the substation-hardened application platform running a Fortinet next-generation firewall payload — with CVE-2026-23573 (6.1, cross-site scripting) and CVE-2026-59839 (5.5, path traversal) affecting all versions; Siemens has published no fixed version either and points customers at support and Fortinet workarounds. Neither is reported as exploited, but both need tracking as open items rather than closed patch tickets, and an APE1808 sits at a substation boundary rather than in a data centre rack.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-225-04 and ICSA-26-225-06

items.title: ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 exposes configuration without authentication — and one endpoint can be used to turn off the audit trail
items.content_text: ICSA-26-225-05 covers ANDRITZ HIPASE-250 and 250 SCALA below version 8.00, a protection and control platform used in hydro and substation applications. Three issues: CVE-2026-65309 (7.5) stores and transmits passwords in a recoverable form, CVE-2026-65310 (7.5) exposes a data and configuration endpoint without authentication and with permissive cross-origin settings, and CVE-2026-65311 (5.3) is an undocumented, unauthenticated logging-configuration endpoint that can be used to suppress the audit trail. Version 8.00 fixes all three. Separately, ICSA-26-225-01 covers AVEVA Enterprise SCADA and Enterprise HMI (CVE-2025-7639, 7.1), where an authenticated DNA Authority Operator can tamper with serialized data and potentially execute code; patched builds exist, but AVEVA also advises moving serialization from BinaryFormatter to JSON, which is change-controlled engineering work rather than a patch window.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-225-05 and ICSA-26-225-01

items.title: Six flaws in CISA’s own Malcolm OT traffic-analysis suite — the worst gives arbitrary code execution
items.content_text: ICSA-26-230-01, published on 18 August, documents six vulnerabilities plus a resource-exhaustion condition in Malcolm, the open-source network traffic analysis suite CISA itself publishes for OT monitoring. The most serious is CVE-2026-55676 (CVSS 8.8), an unrestricted file upload that allows arbitrary code execution; the others are CVE-2026-63177 (7.1, path traversal during archive extraction), CVE-2026-63133 and CVE-2026-19671 (6.5 each), and CVE-2026-63134 and CVE-2026-19670 (5.4 each, authorisation bypasses via unnormalised URI paths and percent-encoding). Compression-bomb inputs can also exhaust resources. Affected releases run below 26.06.1 and 26.07.0 and up to 26.07.1, with fixes in 26.07.0 and 26.08.0 depending on the CVE. This matters more than a typical utility-software advisory because Malcolm is a common low-cost way for utilities to get passive visibility: it usually sits inside the OT network on a SPAN or TAP feed, seeing everything, which makes it a high-value host rather than a peripheral tool. No exploitation is reported.

items.title: A Windows IKE double free is in KEV with a 21 August deadline — and IKE is what terminates your site-to-site tunnels
items.content_text: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August, all with a 21 August federal remediation deadline. The one that matters most for utility networks is CVE-2026-33824, a double free in the Microsoft Windows IKE service extensions (IKEEXT) leading to remote code execution. A three-day deadline is CISA’s signal for active, broad exploitation. The relevance is architectural rather than exotic: IKEEXT is the Windows component that negotiates IPsec, and IPsec is what terminates a large share of utility site-to-site links to substations, remote generation and control-centre backups, as well as vendor and engineer remote access. The same KEV batch added the VMware vCenter path traversal already covered on this page, a SharePoint authentication-bypass flaw and a macOS Screen Sharing authentication flaw.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 18 Aug 2026; remediation deadline 21 Aug 2026

items.title: CIP-012-2 is in force, CIP-003-9 has been enforceable since April, and the 2026 roadmap points at low-impact and cloud
items.content_text: Two compliance dates have already passed this year and both change day-to-day practice. CIP-003-9 became enforceable on 1 April, extending governance expectations to low-impact BES cyber systems with an explicit focus on vendor remote access and supply chain. CIP-012-2 took effect on 1 July, tightening protection of real-time operational data exchanged between control centres. Looking ahead, NERC’s CIP Roadmap published in January sets out near-term standards work and widens the scope conversation to low-impact systems, cloud services, telecommunications and DER aggregators, while FERC has directed NERC to extend internal network security monitoring under CIP-015 to EACMS and PACS. Penalties remain up to $1 million per violation per day, but the operational point is that low-impact sites and vendor access are where the next audit attention lands.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: NERC CIP Roadmap (Jan 2026) and standard effective dates — summarised by Ampyx Cyber and Tenable
_otthreatfeed.date_note: CIP-003-9 effective 1 Apr 2026; CIP-012-2 effective 1 Jul 2026; roadmap Jan 2026

items.title: A new Senate bill would put quantum risk to the bulk electric system inside FERC’s reliability remit — with OT written into scope
items.content_text: The Quantum Grid Utility Assurance and Resilient Defense Act, or Quantum-GUARD Act, was introduced on 18 August by Senators Chris Coons and Mike Rounds. It would direct FERC to assess quantum-related vulnerabilities using its existing reliability authority, require the Department of Energy to study quantum risk to the bulk electric system with operational technology explicitly in scope alongside IT, and establish a DOE test environment for migrating to post-quantum cryptography. The status matters: it has been introduced, not enacted, and creates no obligation today. The practical significance for operators is that a federal proposal is now naming OT rather than treating cryptographic migration as an IT project — which is where the hard problems sit, given protection relays, RTUs and substation gateways with fifteen-to-twenty-year service lives and firmware that cannot readily accept new algorithms.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Bill introduced in the US Senate — reported by The Quantum Insider

items.title: The new National Security Science and Technology Strategy names OT/ICS resilience as a priority
items.content_text: The National Security Science and Technology Strategy was released on 19 August and sets out four pillars, with operational technology and industrial control system resilience and technology supply chains named as explicit priorities rather than folded into a general cybersecurity heading. It is a strategy document: it directs federal research and coordination priorities and creates no operator obligation, no reporting requirement and no compliance date. Its value to a utility is as a signal of where federal attention and funding are being pointed, and as language you can borrow when making an internal case — a national strategy naming control-system resilience and supply chain is useful supporting material for a programme that has to be argued for annually.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: National Security Science & Technology Strategy — summarised by Industrial Cyber
